sections.title: 3. How BFS Works ( Step by Step)

blocks.text: Go level by level. BFS is the go-to algorithm for shortest paths in unweighted graphs, level-order traversal, and anything that demands exploring neighbours before going deeper.
In the previous article we covered DFS go as deep as possible, then backtrack.
BFS takes the opposite approach: explore all neighbours at the current level before moving deeper.
This one difference makes BFS the right choice whenever you need the shortest path in an unweighted graph.

BFS uses a Queue (FIFO) instead of a stack. Every node you discover gets added to the back of the queue, and you always process from the front guaranteeing that closer nodes are always visited before farther ones.

Breadth-First Search starts at a source node and explores the graph in rings all nodes at distance 1, then all at distance 2, then distance 3, and so on. Think of dropping a stone in still water the ripple expands level by level.

KEY INTUITION: BFS is like sending search parties outward from a base camp. First you check everything 1 step away. Then everything 2 steps away. You never send a party 3 steps out until the 2-step zones are all checked.

Start with the source node
Enqueue it and mark it visited.

Dequeue and process
Remove the front node from the queue and process it.

Add unvisited neighbours

Handle disconnected graphs
Start BFS from any unvisited node to cover all components.

blocks.text: Each level = one more edge away from the source. This is exactly the shortest distance from node 1.
STANDARD BFS
(Order can slightly vary depending on adjacency list order.)

COMMON MISTAKE: Mark nodes as visited when you enqueue them not when you dequeue. If you wait until dequeue, the same node can get added to the queue multiple times, causing repeated processing and wrong distances.
<hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">
BFS WITH SHORTEST DISTANCE
Since BFS visits nodes level by level, tracking the distance to each node is straightforward just increment the distance by 1 each time you move to the next level.

blocks.text: Time and Space Complexity
BFS visits every vertex and every edge exactly once same as DFS.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406028612-953174197.png
BFS space depends on the width of the graph (max nodes at any level), while DFS space depends on the depth. For very wide, shallow graphs BFS uses more memory. For deep, narrow graphs DFS uses more.

• Level / Layer All nodes at the same shortest distance from the source. BFS naturally groups nodes into levels.
  • BFS tree The spanning tree formed by the edges BFS uses to discover new nodes. Every tree edge goes from level L to level L+1.
  • Shortest path In an unweighted graph, BFS guarantees the path it finds is the shortest (fewest edges). This is its biggest advantage over DFS.
  • Cross edge An edge between two nodes at the same level. BFS never uses cross edges to discover new nodes they connect already-visited nodes at the same depth.
  • Multi-source BFS Start BFS from multiple nodes simultaneously by enqueuing all sources at the start. Used for problems like "distance to nearest 0 in a grid".
  • 0-1 BFS A variant using a deque instead of a queue. Used when edges have weights of only 0 or 1. Runs in O(V + E) like regular BFS.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406028612-181988778.png
BFS tree distances from source are guaranteed to be shortest. Cross edges connect same-level nodes but are never used to discover them.

blocks.text: 7. Where BFS Shows Up

• Shortest path Find the fewest edges between two nodes in an unweighted graph.
  • Grid / maze solving Find the shortest path in a 2D grid by treating cells as graph nodes.
  • Web crawling Crawl web pages level by level starting from a seed URL.
  • Social networks Compute degrees of separation (e.g., friends of friends).
  • Bipartite check Two-color the graph level by level; same-color neighbors indicate it's not bipartite.
  • Kahn's topological sort BFS using nodes with in-degree 0 to process dependencies.
